title: Treatment for acute anterior cruciate ligament tear: five year outcome of randomised trial
question: In young, active adults with an acute ACL tear, does rehabilitation plus early reconstruction give better five year results than rehabilitation with the option of a later reconstruction?

bottom_line.question: In young, active adults with an acute ACL tear, does rehabilitation plus early reconstruction give better five year results than rehabilitation with the option of a later reconstruction?
bottom_line.answer: Five years after an acute ACL tear, the KOOS4 knee score improved by 42.9 points with early reconstruction and 44.9 points with rehabilitation plus optional later reconstruction, a difference of 2.0 points that was not statistically significant.

provenance.quote: the mean change in KOOS4 score from baseline to five years was 42.9 points for patients assigned to rehabilitation plus early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and 44.9 points for those assigned to rehabilitation plus optional delayed reconstruction (between group difference 2.0 points, 95% confidence interval −8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54 after adjustment for the baseline score)

sections.title: The Question: Surgery or Rehabilitation After an ACL Tear
sections.markdown:
The **anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)** is one of the main ligaments in the knee. It connects the thigh bone to the shin bone and stops the shin from sliding forward. Young, active people tear it often, and it is a serious injury. Many end up with a knee that feels unstable, do less physical activity, and rate their knee-related quality of life lower. Many also develop knee osteoarthritis later on, whichever treatment they had.

There are two main ways to treat it. In surgical reconstruction, a surgeon replaces the torn ligament with a graft taken from one of the patient's own tendons, and the patient then does rehabilitation. The other option is structured rehabilitation (guided exercise and physiotherapy), with surgery held back for patients whose knee keeps giving way. Surgery is commonly recommended for people who want to get back to sport. How much it adds over rehabilitation is still debated, and there has been little trial evidence to settle it.

The KANON trial in Sweden compared the two strategies head to head. Its two-year results found no difference in how patients rated their knees. This report follows the same patients to five years and adds X-ray evidence of osteoarthritis and a count of meniscus operations. The authors say it is the first randomised trial to compare these strategies over the medium term.

sections.title: How the Trial Worked
sections.markdown:
The researchers enrolled 121 adults aged 18 to 35 (average age 26) at two Swedish hospitals. Each had torn the ACL in the previous four weeks, in a knee with no earlier injury. The trial excluded professional athletes, people who were less than moderately active, and people with certain other major knee damage, such as a complete tear of a collateral ligament or a full-thickness cartilage defect on MRI.

In a **randomised controlled trial**, chance decides which treatment each person gets. That makes the groups alike at the start, so later differences can be put down to the treatment. Patients were assigned to one of two strategies:

- **Early reconstruction:** 62 patients had rehabilitation plus ACL surgery within 10 weeks of the injury.
- **Rehabilitation with optional delayed reconstruction:** 59 patients had the same rehabilitation and could have surgery later if the knee became unstable. The protocol defined instability as symptoms caused by the missing ACL together with a positive pivot shift test, an exam in which the doctor bends and rotates the knee to check whether the shin bone slips out of place.

Four experienced knee surgeons did all the operations. Each chose between a graft from the patellar tendon (just below the kneecap) and a graft from the hamstring tendons. In both groups, torn menisci were trimmed or repaired when needed. The menisci are the two rubbery cartilage pads that cushion the inside of the knee.

Only one patient was lost to follow-up by five years, so 120 of 121 were analysed. Long-term surgical studies rarely keep that many patients, and it makes the results more trustworthy.

sections.title: What They Measured
sections.markdown:
The main outcome came from the **knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS)**, a questionnaire in which patients rate their own knee. It has five subscales, each scored from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). The trial averaged four of them into one number:

KOOS4 = (sum of four KOOS subscale scores) / 4

The primary result was how much that number improved:

main outcome = KOOS4 at five years minus KOOS4 at the start

The trial enrolled about 120 patients so it would have an 80% chance of detecting a 10-point difference between the groups on this measure.

Secondary outcomes included:

- the SF-36, a general health survey with a physical score and a mental score
- the Tegner activity scale (1 to 10), plus whether patients got back to their pre-injury activity level
- knee stability on two clinical tests, the Lachman and the pivot shift
- **radiographic osteoarthritis**, meaning signs of joint wear on standing X-rays. A radiologist who did not know each patient's treatment graded the X-rays, separately for the joint between the thigh and shin bones (tibiofemoral) and the joint behind the kneecap (patellofemoral)
- meniscus surgery over the five years

The data were analysed in two ways. The **full analysis set** compares patients by the group they were randomly assigned to. The "as treated" analysis compares them by the treatment they actually received. The second matters here because many patients in the rehabilitation group had surgery later.

sections.title: Five-Year Results
sections.markdown:
### Half the rehabilitation group never had surgery

Of the 59 patients assigned to rehabilitation first, 30 (51%) had a delayed reconstruction. Seven of those operations happened between two and five years after the injury. The other 29 were treated with rehabilitation alone. Over the whole study, 61 patients had early reconstruction, 30 had delayed reconstruction, and 29 never had surgery.

### Patients rated their knees the same

KOOS4 improved by 42.9 points in the early surgery group and by 44.9 points in the rehabilitation-first group. The reported difference was 2.0 points, with a 95% confidence interval of −8.5 to 4.5 (P = 0.54). A confidence interval is the range of true differences the data are consistent with. This one includes zero, and both ends fall short of the 10-point difference the trial was designed to detect. The P value is how likely a gap this size would be by chance if the treatments were equal. At 0.54, it is far above the usual 0.05 cut-off for statistical significance.

At five years, there were also no significant differences in:

- KOOS4 itself (P = 0.45)
- any of the five KOOS subscales (P ≥ 0.12)
- SF-36 (P ≥ 0.34)
- Tegner activity level (P = 0.74)
- return to pre-injury activity

The as-treated analysis gave similar results (Table 3). Knees rebuilt early, knees rebuilt late and knees treated with rehabilitation alone all came out much the same.

### Surgery gave a more stable knee on examination

Knees assigned to early reconstruction were more stable on both the Lachman and the pivot shift tests (both P < 0.001). That better stability did not show up in patients' own ratings of pain, function, activity or quality of life.

### Osteoarthritis appeared early whatever the treatment

Both sets of X-rays (start and five years) were available for 113 knees. None showed osteoarthritis at the start. After five years, 13 knees (12%) had tibiofemoral osteoarthritis and 22 (19%) had patellofemoral osteoarthritis, with 6 knees showing both. The randomised groups did not differ significantly (P = 0.17), and neither did the as-treated groups.

Among the 87 reconstructed knees, 11% had tibiofemoral and 23% had patellofemoral osteoarthritis. Among the 26 knees treated with rehabilitation alone, the figures were 12% and 8%. The patellofemoral gap was not statistically significant (P = 0.084). Graft type did matter. Knees rebuilt with a patellar tendon graft had significantly more patellofemoral osteoarthritis than knees rebuilt with hamstring grafts (P = 0.001). The authors point to two possible causes: the patellar tendon can shorten after surgery, which changes the load on the kneecap joint, and the bone where the graft was taken remodels as it heals.

The authors call it striking that this much osteoarthritis appears within five years in people around 30 years old. They conclude that reconstructing the ACL does not protect the knee from these structural changes.

### Meniscus surgery and graft ruptures

A common argument for operating early is that an unstable knee damages the menisci over time. Earlier observational studies found more meniscus injuries when surgery was delayed. The authors note those studies are "confounded by indication": patients who delay surgery may differ in other ways from those who don't.

In this trial, 61 knees (51%) had meniscus surgery during the five years: 29 in the early surgery group and 32 in the rehabilitation-first group (P = 0.48). A time-to-event analysis, which tracks when each meniscus was first operated on and compares the two groups over time, also found no difference (P = 0.77). When repeat operations on the same meniscus were counted, the early surgery group had fewer procedures in total. This was an exploratory analysis reported in the supplementary appendix.

Grafts tore in 3 of 61 early reconstructions (5%) and 1 of 30 delayed reconstructions (3%). That matches the 4.3% rupture rate reported in a five-year follow-up of 1415 reconstruction patients. Two of the four patients chose a second (revision) operation.

sections.title: What It Means for Patients and Clinicians
sections.markdown:
At five years, starting with rehabilitation and keeping surgery as an option did as well as early reconstruction on patient-reported outcomes, X-ray osteoarthritis and meniscus surgery. Half the patients who started with rehabilitation never needed a reconstruction. The trial found no evidence that either strategy did more harm than the other. Early surgery gave better stability on clinical tests, but patients did not report better function because of it.

The authors conclude that clinicians and young active adults should consider rehabilitation as a first-line treatment after an acute ACL tear. The findings do not apply to professional athletes or to people who are less than moderately active, since the trial excluded both groups. Because osteoarthritis can take many years to develop, the authors call for continued long-term follow-up of this and other groups of patients treated with and without surgery.

anchors.quote: We found statistically significantly more patellofemoral radiographic osteoarthritis (P=0.001), but not tibiofemoral radiographic osteoarthritis (P=0.269), in knees reconstructed using patella tendon procedures compared with hamstrings tendon procedures.

anchors.sentence: The authors point to two possible causes: the patellar tendon can shorten after surgery, which changes the load on the kneecap joint, and the bone where the graft was taken remodels as it heals.
The authors call it striking that this much osteoarthritis appears within five years in people around 30 years old.
anchors.quote: The high frequency of radiographic osteoarthritis of the knee already at five years after anterior cruciate ligament injury at an age of about 30 is striking, and the results of this study indicate that surgical reconstruction of the torn anterior cruciate ligament does not protect the injured knee from developing structural changes consistent with osteoarthritis.

anchors.sentence: They conclude that reconstructing the ACL does not protect the knee from these structural changes.

anchors.sentence: A common argument for operating early is that an unstable knee damages the menisci over time.
anchors.quote: We report the number of index knees with meniscus surgery over the five year period and the proportion of meniscuses operated on (assuming two intact meniscuses in every index knee before injury) by using a “time to event” analysis.

anchors.sentence: Earlier observational studies found more meniscus injuries when surgery was delayed.
anchors.quote: When we accounted for repeated surgery on the same meniscus, we found a lower frequency of meniscus surgery procedures in patients treated with rehabilitation plus early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction compared with those treated with initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later reconstruction (supplementary appendix).

anchors.sentence: The authors note those studies are "confounded by indication": patients who delay surgery may differ in other ways from those who don't.
In this trial, 61 knees (51%) had meniscus surgery during the five years: 29 in the early surgery group and 32 in the rehabilitation-first group (P = 0.48).
anchors.quote: Sixty one (51%) knees, 29 treated with early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and 32 treated with initial rehabilitation with the option of a later reconstruction, had meniscus surgery over the five year period, with no statistically significant difference between the groups (P=0.483).

anchors.sentence: A time-to-event analysis, which tracks when each meniscus was first operated on and compares the two groups over time, also found no difference (P = 0.77).
anchors.quote: We found no statistically significant differences in a time to event analysis of the proportion of meniscuses operated on for the full analysis set (P=0.774; fig 2) or in the as treated comparison (P=0.210; fig 3).

anchors.sentence: This was an exploratory analysis reported in the supplementary appendix.
anchors.quote: In addition, we report the proportion of meniscuses operated on and the total number of meniscus surgeries (including repeat surgery on either meniscus) at five years as exploratory outcomes in the supplementary appendix.

anchors.sentence: Grafts tore in 3 of 61 early reconstructions (5%) and 1 of 30 delayed reconstructions (3%).
anchors.quote: In this study, three of the 61 (5%) knees treated with early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, and one (3%) of the 30 knees treated with delayed reconstruction had a new severe injury resulting in a graft rupture over the five year period.

anchors.sentence: That matches the 4.3% rupture rate reported in a five-year follow-up of 1415 reconstruction patients.
anchors.quote: These results are consistent with the 4.3% graft rupture rate reported from a five year follow-up of 1415 patients treated with anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

anchors.sentence: Two of the four patients chose a second (revision) operation.
At five years, starting with rehabilitation and keeping surgery as an option did as well as early reconstruction on patient-reported outcomes, X-ray osteoarthritis and meniscus surgery.
anchors.quote: In this five year prospective trial, we have shown that in young, active adults with an acute anterior cruciate ligament tear, a strategy of early reconstruction plus rehabilitation did not provide better results, whether measured as patient reported outcomes, radiographic osteoarthritis, or meniscus surgery, than a strategy of initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.

anchors.sentence: Half the patients who started with rehabilitation never needed a reconstruction.
The trial found no evidence that either strategy did more harm than the other.
anchors.quote: Over the five year observation time of this trial, we did not find any evidence of one treatment being more harmful than the other.

anchors.sentence: Early surgery gave better stability on clinical tests, but patients did not report better function because of it.
anchors.quote: Knee stability at rest at five years was statistically significantly better in knees assigned to early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction compared with those assigned to initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later reconstruction if needed, as indicated by normal Lachman (P<0.001) and pivot shift (P<0.001) tests (table 2).

anchors.sentence: The authors conclude that clinicians and young active adults should consider rehabilitation as a first-line treatment after an acute ACL tear.
anchors.quote: These results should encourage clinicians and young active adult patients to consider rehabilitation as a primary treatment option after an acute ACL tear.

anchors.sentence: The findings do not apply to professional athletes or to people who are less than moderately active, since the trial excluded both groups.

anchors.sentence: Because osteoarthritis can take many years to develop, the authors call for continued long-term follow-up of this and other groups of patients treated with and without surgery.
anchors.quote: Acute anterior cruciate ligament injury may lead to unsatisfactory knee function, decreased activity, and poor knee related quality of life, and many patients with a torn anterior cruciate ligament develop osteoarthritis of the knee irrespective of treatment.

We found no statistically significant differences in KOOS4, any of the five individual subscales of KOOS, SF-36, or Tegner activity scale between the two treatment strategies at five years or in the change between two and five years (table 2). sources.abstract: Objective To compare, in young active adults with an acute anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, the mid-term (five year) patient reported and radiographic outcomes between those treated with rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction and those treated with rehabilitation and optional delayed ACL reconstruction. Design Extended follow-up of prospective randomised controlled trial. Setting Orthopaedic departments at two hospitals in Sweden. Participants 121 young, active adults (mean age 26 years) with acute ACL injury to a previously uninjured knee. One patient was lost to five year follow-up. Intervention All patients received similar structured rehabilitation. In addition to rehabilitation, 62 patients were assigned to early ACL reconstruction and 59 were assigned to the option of having a delayed ACL reconstruction if needed. Main outcome measure The main outcome was the change from baseline to five years in the mean value of four of the five subscales of the knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS4). Other outcomes included the absolute KOOS4 score, all five KOOS subscale scores, SF-36, Tegner activity scale, meniscal surgery, and radiographic osteoarthritis at five years. Results Thirty (51%) patients assigned to optional delayed ACL reconstruction had delayed ACL reconstruction (seven between two and five years). The mean change in KOOS4 score from baseline to five years was 42.9 points for those assigned to rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction and 44.9 for those assigned to rehabilitation plus optional delayed reconstruction (between group difference 2.0 points, 95% confidence interval −8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54 after adjustment for baseline score). At five years, no significant between group differences were seen in KOOS4 (P=0.45), any of the KOOS subscales (P≥0.12), SF-36 (P≥0.34), Tegner activity scale (P=0.74), or incident radiographic osteoarthritis of the index knee (P=0.17). sources.sec-characteristics-of-patients-and-trea: Despite several contacts by mail and telephone, one patient assigned to early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction did not attend the five year clinical visit. Consequently, we included 120/121 participants in this five year follow-up report, 61 of whom were assigned to early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction and 59 to initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later reconstruction if needed (table 1). Two patients assigned to early reconstruction did not have reconstruction or had less than 10 rehabilitation visits; we excluded them from the as treated analysis but included them in the full analysis set.

Thirty (51%) patients assigned to initial rehabilitation with the option of having a later reconstruction chose to have (and had) a delayed anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction over the five year period (seven in the period between two and five years; median 867 (range 743-1695) days after injury) (fig 1). Fifteen anterior cruciate ligaments were reconstructed using patella tendon procedures and 15 using hamstrings tendon procedures. Over the five year period, 61 patients had an early anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction, 30 had a delayed reconstruction, and 29 were treated with rehabilitation alone. Of the 91 primary reconstructions performed, 40 used patella tendon procedures and 51 used hamstrings tendon procedures.
sources.sec-patient-reported-outcomes-5/p1: Patient reported outcomes included the knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score (KOOS), the Medical Outcomes Study 36-item short-form health survey (SF-36), and the Tegner activity scale. Consistent with our previous publication, the main outcome of this report was the change from baseline to five years in the mean value of four of the five KOOS subscales (KOOS4). Other outcomes include the crude KOOS4 score, all five separate KOOS subscales, the scores on the SF-36 physical and mental components (all 0-100 scales, worst to best), and the Tegner activity scale score (1-10, lowest to highest) at five years. In addition, we report return to pre-injury activity level as patients who reported similar or higher Tegner activity scale scores at five years compared with their pre-injury scores.
sources.sec-participants-3/p1: We enrolled active adults, 18 to 35 years of age, with an anterior cruciate ligament tear not more than four weeks old to a previously uninjured knee at the departments of orthopaedics at Skåne University Hospital and Helsingborg Hospital, Sweden (table 1). Major exclusion criteria were professional athletes (10 on the Tegner activity score; 0-10, lowest to highest activity level), less than moderately active people (<5 on the same scale), a total collateral ligament rupture, a full thickness cartilage lesion visualised on magnetic resonance imaging, and extensive meniscal fixation. Details of the recruitment process, full inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the randomisation process have been published. All patients provided fully informed written consent to participate in the study.
sources.sec-knee-radiography-and-grading-of-imag: We report presence of radiographic osteoarthritis separately for the tibiofemoral and patellofemoral compartments. In agreement with previous reports, we considered radiographic osteoarthritis to be present if any of the following criteria were achieved in either of the medial or lateral tibiofemoral compartments or in the patellofemoral compartment: joint space narrowing grade 2 or above (tibiofemoral compartment only); sum of the two marginal osteophyte grades from the same compartment 2 or above; grade 1 joint space narrowing in combination with grade 1 osteophytes in the same compartment (tibiofemoral compartment only). For the tibiofemoral compartment, this cut-off approximates to grade 2 radiographic osteoarthritis based on the Kellgren and Lawrence scale.
